newsitem.title: USA: Hughes wins contract for new "Sidewinder".
newsitem.headline: Hughes wins contract for new "Sidewinder".

text.p: The U.S. military on Friday awarded a $169.2 million contract to Hughes Missiles Systems Co. to develop a successor to the AIM-9M Sidewinder missile used by fighter jets against enemy aircraft.

GM Hughes, owned by General Motors Corp., won a major competition with Raytheon Co which could eventually mean $5 billion in sales of the short-range AIM-9X and vault the United States ahead of "dog-fighting" missiles built by other nations.
The new heat-seeking air-to-air missile would replace the aging Sidewinder carried by U.S. warplanes and others from 26 nations in various versions for more than 30 years.

The Sidewinder, last updated after the 1991 Gulf War, is the Pentagon's only such short-range missile for Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps fighters and is now considered inferior to other advanced missiles, including Russia's AA-11 "Archer."

The contract awarded to Hughes on Friday was for development of the new AIM-9X over five years and production of 1,000 early missiles. The Pentagon said it could ready a total of $252.5 million if additional development options are exercised during that period.
But actual production will mean far more money. The U.S. military alone is expected to buy at least 10,000 of the new missiles in the next century.

The AIM-9X, like the Sidewinder, will seek out heat signals from target aircraft. But it will be more advanced, according to the Navy, which is the lead contracting agent for the Defense Department on the new program.

Current Sidewinders can be lured off course by flares released by target aircraft. The new missile would reportedly incorporate sensors that not only look at exhaust plume but can see the whole aircraft and would not be fooled by flares.
Both Raytheon and Hughes had proposed two versions of a missile to replace the Sidewinder.
One would be built around the current weapon, using the same motor and warhead to slash costs. The other would be a more costly projectile powered by a powerful motor to reach targets faster.

Even as Raytheon and Hughes Electronics competed over the new missile, General Motors and Raytheon have reportedly been involved in recent talks which could lead to the possible sale of Hughes' defense business to Raytheon.

While is has become necessary to vastly improve the short-range Sidewinder, defense experts say that the United States currently builds the most advanced medium-range air-to-air missile in the world, the AIM-120.
The AIM-120 advanced medium-range air-to-air missile (AMRAAM) is built by both Hughes and Raytheon, but there are currently no plans to use two suppliers for the new short-range missile.
